title: Bug: ArFrame column selection methods drop attrs metadata
body:
## Summary

`ArFrame` preserves pandas `DataFrame.attrs` through `from_pandas()` and `to_pandas()`, but column-selection methods on `ArFrame` drop that metadata.

This affects methods such as `select_columns()`, `drop_columns()`, and `select_dtypes()`, all of which construct `ArFrame(...)` without passing a copy of the source frame attrs.

## Why it matters

Users may store provenance, owner, sensitivity tags, source system names, or run IDs in `DataFrame.attrs`. After converting into Arnio, basic column selection should not silently remove that metadata.

This is separate from native cleaning operations dropping attrs because these are core `ArFrame` methods.

## Evidence

- `arnio/convert.py`: `from_pandas()` deep-copies pandas attrs into `ArFrame`.
- `arnio/convert.py`: `to_pandas()` restores `ArFrame._attrs` to pandas output.
- `arnio/frame.py`: `select_columns()` returns `ArFrame(self._frame.select_columns(columns))` with no attrs.
- `arnio/frame.py`: `drop_columns()` returns `ArFrame(self._frame.select_columns(...))` with no attrs.
- `arnio/frame.py`: `select_dtypes()` delegates to `select_columns()`, so it also drops attrs.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

source = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
source.attrs = {"source": "crm"}

frame = ar.from_pandas(source)
print(frame._attrs)
print(frame.select_columns(["a"])._attrs)
print(frame.drop_columns(["b"])._attrs)
print(frame.select_dtypes(include="int64")._attrs)
```

Current behavior: the original frame has attrs, while selected frames have `{}`.

## Expected behavior

Non-mutating column-selection operations should preserve a defensive copy of `frame._attrs` unless the project explicitly documents that metadata is intentionally discarded.

## Actual behavior

The returned `ArFrame` objects have empty attrs.

## Suggested direction

Add a small helper for wrapping derived native frames with copied attrs and use it in `ArFrame` selection methods. Add tests for:

- `select_columns()` preserving attrs
- `drop_columns()` preserving attrs
- `select_dtypes()` preserving attrs through selection
- deep-copy isolation so nested attrs are not shared unexpectedly

## References

- `arnio/frame.py`
- `arnio/convert.py`
- Related but separate issue: native cleaning wrappers dropping attrs metadata

nodes.title: fix: preserve attrs metadata in ArFrame selection methods
nodes.body: Closes #1661. Ensures select_columns and drop_columns deep copy self._attrs when constructing new ArFrames so metadata is not lost.

title: Bug: read_csv_chunked does not auto-detect TSV delimiters
body:
## Summary

`read_csv()` automatically uses a tab delimiter for `.tsv` files when `delimiter` is omitted, but `read_csv_chunked()` defaults to comma and does not apply the same `.tsv` behavior.

This makes chunked reads parse TSV files as a single column unless the user manually passes `delimiter="\t"`.

## Why it matters

Chunked reading is the path users choose for larger files. It should behave consistently with `read_csv()` for common file types, especially because the `read_csv_chunked()` docs say `.tsv` is supported.

## Evidence

- `arnio/io.py::read_csv()` accepts `delimiter: str | None = None` and sets `"\t"` when the path ends with `.tsv`.
- `arnio/io.py::read_csv_chunked()` uses `delimiter: str = ","` and never checks the `.tsv` extension to choose a tab delimiter.
- A runtime probe with a `.tsv` file returns one column named `'a\tb'` instead of `['a', 'b']`.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
import arnio as ar

path = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "arnio_chunk_probe.tsv"
path.write_text("a\tb\n1\t2\n3\t4\n", encoding="utf-8")

chunk = next(ar.read_csv_chunked(path, chunksize=10))
print(chunk.columns)
print(chunk.to_dict())
```

Current output:

```python
['a\tb']
{'a\tb': ['1\t2', '3\t4']}
```

## Expected behavior

When `delimiter` is omitted and the path ends with `.tsv`, `read_csv_chunked()` should parse with `"\t"`, matching `read_csv()`.

## Actual behavior

It uses comma by default and treats each TSV row as a single field.

## Suggested direction

Change `read_csv_chunked()` so `delimiter` can default to `None`, then apply the same `.tsv` delimiter resolution used by `read_csv()`. Add regression tests for:

- `.tsv` chunked reads with omitted delimiter
- explicit `delimiter=","` still being honored for `.tsv` paths
- parity with `read_csv()` on the same file

## References

- `arnio/io.py::read_csv`
- `arnio/io.py::read_csv_chunked`

title: Bug: CSV readers apply encoding twice for text file-like inputs
body:
## Summary

`read_csv()` and `read_csv_chunked()` support text file-like objects by copying their already-decoded text into a temporary UTF-8 CSV file. However, the rest of the read path still treats that temporary file as if it were encoded with the user-provided `encoding`.

This means text streams can fail or be misinterpreted when `encoding` is not UTF-8, even though text file-like input has already been decoded by the caller.

## Why it matters

Users often pass `io.StringIO`, web framework upload wrappers, or already-decoded text streams into CSV readers. For those inputs, `encoding` should not be applied a second time to the temporary UTF-8 file.

## Evidence

- `arnio/io.py::_materialize_csv_input()` writes file-like text to a temporary file with `encoding="utf-8"`.
- `arnio/io.py::read_csv()` later calls `_utf8_csv_path(path, encoding, ...)` using the original user-supplied `encoding`.
- `arnio/io.py::read_csv_chunked()` follows the same materialize-then-transcode path.
- For text streams, that can decode the UTF-8 temp file as another encoding.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import io
import arnio as ar

csv = io.StringIO("name\ncafé\n")
ar.read_csv(csv, encoding="utf-16")
```

Current behavior raises:

```text
CsvReadError: Could not decode '<temp>.csv' using encoding 'utf-16'
```

## Expected behavior

For text file-like inputs, Arnio should treat the materialized temporary file as UTF-8 because the stream has already produced Python strings.

## Actual behavior

The original `encoding` is applied again to the UTF-8 temp file.

## Suggested direction

Have `_materialize_csv_input()` return enough metadata to distinguish original filesystem paths from materialized text streams. When the source is a text file-like object, use UTF-8 for subsequent temp-file validation/transcoding regardless of the caller's `encoding`.

Add tests for:

- `io.StringIO` with `encoding="utf-16"`
- `io.StringIO` with non-ASCII text
- `read_csv_chunked()` with the same file-like scenario
- filesystem path input still honoring `encoding`
- temporary file cleanup on decoding errors

## References

- `arnio/io.py::_materialize_csv_input`
- `arnio/io.py::read_csv`
- `arnio/io.py::read_csv_chunked`
- `arnio/io.py::_utf8_csv_path`

title: Bug: sniff_delimiter rejects valid UTF-16 CSV files as binary
body:
## Summary

`sniff_delimiter()` rejects valid UTF-16 CSV files before decoding them because it always calls the raw NUL-byte binary check.

UTF-16 text commonly contains NUL bytes in its byte representation, so the current check incorrectly treats valid encoded CSV text as corrupted binary input.

## Why it matters

`read_csv()` supports explicit encodings. Users should be able to sniff delimiters for encoded CSV files before reading them, especially when working with exports from Excel, Windows tools, or enterprise systems that may use UTF-16.

## Evidence

- `arnio/io.py::sniff_delimiter()` calls `_reject_utf8_nul_bytes(path)` unconditionally.
- `_reject_utf8_nul_bytes()` is appropriate for raw UTF-8 input, but not for UTF-16/UTF-32 encoded text.
- A valid UTF-16 CSV fails before the sample is opened with `encoding="utf-16"`.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile
import arnio as ar

path = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "arnio_utf16_sniff.csv"
path.write_text("a,b\n1,2\n", encoding="utf-16")

print(ar.sniff_delimiter(path, encoding="utf-16"))
```

Current behavior:

```text
CsvReadError: CSV input contains NUL bytes and appears to be binary or corrupted
```

## Expected behavior

For non-UTF-8 encodings, `sniff_delimiter()` should decode the sample using the requested encoding and then inspect the decoded text.

## Actual behavior

It rejects the file as binary before decoding.

## Suggested direction

Make the NUL-byte binary check encoding-aware, similar to the CSV read path. Only apply raw NUL-byte rejection when the requested encoding is UTF-8-compatible, or move corruption detection after decoding for non-UTF-8 inputs.

Add tests for:

- UTF-16 comma-delimited CSV delimiter sniffing
- UTF-16 tab-delimited CSV delimiter sniffing
- UTF-8 binary/NUL input still being rejected
- invalid encoding errors remaining clear

## References

- `arnio/io.py::sniff_delimiter`
- `arnio/io.py::_reject_utf8_nul_bytes`
- `arnio/io.py::_is_utf8_encoding`

title: Bug: diff_schema ignores cross-field validation rules
body:
## Summary

`diff_schema()` compares fields, `strict`, and `unique`, but it ignores `Schema.rules`. Two schemas can have different cross-field validation behavior and still be reported as unchanged.

## Why it matters

Cross-field rules are part of the schema contract. If `diff_schema()` is used in CI or release checks, missing or changed rules can silently pass as no schema drift.

## Evidence

- `arnio/schema.py::Schema` accepts a `rules` list of callables.
- `arnio/schema.py::validate()` executes `schema.rules` after field and uniqueness checks.
- `arnio/schema.py::diff_schema()` does not inspect or report `rules` at all.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import arnio as ar

def rule_a(df):
    return []

expected = ar.Schema({"x": ar.Int64()}, rules=[rule_a])
observed = ar.Schema({"x": ar.Int64()}, rules=None)

print(ar.diff_schema(expected, observed).to_dict())
```

Current output:

```python
{'changed': False, 'difference_count': 0, 'differences': []}
```

## Expected behavior

`diff_schema()` should report that schema-level validation rules differ when one schema has rules and the other does not, or when the visible rule identity/count differs.

## Actual behavior

Rule differences are ignored entirely.

## Suggested direction

Add a schema-level comparison for `rules`. A minimal contributor-friendly version could compare:

- rule count
- callable `__name__` values where available
- presence/absence of rules

The diff entry can use `change="changed_schema"` and `attribute="rules"`. If exact callable equality is intentionally unsupported, document that the comparison is best-effort by name/count.

Add tests for:

- rules present vs absent
- same rule name/count reporting unchanged
- different rule names reporting changed
- `to_markdown()` rendering the schema-level rules difference clearly

## References

- `arnio/schema.py::Schema`
- `arnio/schema.py::validate`
- `arnio/schema.py::diff_schema`

title: Bug: register_validator silently overwrites existing custom validators
body:
## Summary

`register_validator()` silently replaces an existing validator when the same name is registered again. Because `Custom()` stores the validator name as `semantic="custom:<name>"`, already-created schemas use the latest function in the global registry, not the function that existed when the schema was created.

This can silently change validation results for existing schema objects.

## Why it matters

Custom validators are part of production data contracts. Accidental name reuse should not mutate validation behavior globally without an explicit opt-in.

## Evidence

- `arnio/schema.py::_CUSTOM_VALIDATORS` is a global registry.
- `arnio/schema.py::register_validator()` assigns `_CUSTOM_VALIDATORS[name] = fn` with no duplicate-name guard.
- `arnio/schema.py::Custom()` stores only the validator name in the field semantic.
- Runtime behavior changes for an existing schema after re-registering the same validator name.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

ar.register_validator("tmp_probe", lambda value: True)
schema = ar.Schema({"x": ar.Custom("tmp_probe")})
frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"x": ["bad"]}))

print(ar.validate(frame, schema).passed)  # True

ar.register_validator("tmp_probe", lambda value: False)
print(ar.validate(frame, schema).passed)  # False
```

## Expected behavior

Registering a duplicate validator name should fail by default, or require an explicit `overwrite=True` argument.

## Actual behavior

The second registration silently replaces the first function and changes validation behavior for existing schemas.

## Suggested direction

Mirror the pipeline registry pattern:

- reject duplicate validator names by default
- optionally support `overwrite=True` for deliberate replacement
- add tests showing existing schemas are not changed accidentally
- document the overwrite behavior if it is supported

## References

- `arnio/schema.py::register_validator`
- `arnio/schema.py::Custom`
- `arnio/schema.py::_CUSTOM_VALIDATORS`

title: Bug: validate core ValidationIssue field types
body:
## Summary

`ValidationIssue` is a public dataclass but does not validate core field types such as `column`, `rule`, `message`, or `row_index`. Invalid values can be stored and later break report generation methods like `ValidationResult.summary()`.

This is separate from validating the `severity` value.

## Why it matters

Custom schema rules return `ValidationIssue` objects. If a rule accidentally creates malformed issues, Arnio should fail early with a clear error instead of allowing invalid report objects that break later during summary/Markdown/export operations.

## Evidence

- `arnio/schema.py::ValidationIssue` has no `__post_init__` validation.
- `arnio/schema.py::ValidationResult.summary()` assumes `issue.rule` is hashable and string-like.
- Custom rule validation checks that returned items are `ValidationIssue` instances, but not whether their fields are valid.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import arnio as ar

issue = ar.ValidationIssue(
    column=123,
    rule=["not", "hashable"],
    message=5,
    row_index="row1",
)

result = ar.ValidationResult(
    row_count=1,
    issue_count=1,
    issues=[issue],
    bad_rows=["row1"],
)

print(issue.to_dict())
print(result.summary())
```

Current behavior:

```text
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
```

## Expected behavior

`ValidationIssue` should reject invalid field types at construction time with clear errors.

## Actual behavior

Invalid values are accepted and fail later in unrelated reporting code.

## Suggested direction

Add `ValidationIssue.__post_init__()` checks for:

- `column` is `str | None`
- `rule` is a non-empty `str`
- `message` is a `str`
- `row_index` is `int | None` and non-negative or 1-based according to the project convention
- keep the existing severity validation behavior aligned with the separate severity issue

Add tests for direct construction and for custom rule outputs.

## References

- `arnio/schema.py::ValidationIssue`
- `arnio/schema.py::ValidationResult.summary`
- `arnio/schema.py::validate`

nodes.body:
Fixes #1667

## Summary

`ValidationIssue` previously accepted invalid field values silently, which could later break reporting methods such as `ValidationResult.summary()` and `to_markdown()` with cryptic runtime errors. This PR adds early validation in `ValidationIssue.__post_init__()` so malformed issues fail immediately with clear, actionable errors instead of propagating into unrelated reporting code.

Added validation for:
- `column` → `str | None`
- `rule` → non-empty `str`
- `message` → `str`
- `row_index` → `int | None` and non-negative

`bool` values are explicitly rejected for `row_index` since `bool` is a subclass of `int` in Python. Existing severity validation behavior through `_validate_severity()` remains unchanged.

Also added regression tests covering:
- invalid field types for each core field
- valid boundary cases
- the original reproduction scenario from the issue
- malformed `ValidationIssue` objects returned from custom schema rules

title: Bug: DataQualityReport.to_pandas should return stable columns for empty reports
body:
## Summary

`DataQualityReport.to_pandas()` returns a DataFrame with no columns when the report has no profiled columns. This makes the export schema unstable for empty or fully excluded reports.

## Why it matters

Quality reports are often consumed by notebooks, CI summaries, dashboards, or tests. Even when there are no columns to report, the DataFrame export should have a predictable set of column names so downstream code can select/report fields safely.

## Evidence

- `arnio/quality.py::DataQualityReport.to_pandas()` builds `pd.DataFrame([...])` directly from `self.columns.values()`.
- When `self.columns` is empty, pandas receives an empty list and creates a `(0, 0)` DataFrame.
- `ValidationResult.to_pandas()` already handles the analogous case by returning stable issue columns for passing results.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame(index=range(2)))
report = ar.profile(frame)

print(report.to_pandas().columns.tolist())
print(report.to_pandas().shape)
```

Current output:

```python
[]
(0, 0)
```

## Expected behavior

`to_pandas()` should return an empty DataFrame with the documented report columns, such as `name`, `dtype`, `semantic_type`, `null_count`, `unique_count`, `warnings`, and related metric fields.

## Actual behavior

It returns a DataFrame with no columns.

## Suggested direction

Define a stable list of quality-report export columns and pass it to `pd.DataFrame(..., columns=...)` when there are no column profiles.

Add tests for:

- zero-column reports
- reports where all columns are excluded
- normal reports preserving existing columns and values

## References

- `arnio/quality.py::DataQualityReport.to_pandas`
- `arnio/schema.py::ValidationResult.to_pandas`

title: Bug: validate normalize_unicode form type before membership check
body:
## Summary
`normalize_unicode()` should validate that `form` is a string before checking membership in the supported normalization-form set. Passing an unhashable value such as a list currently raises Python's raw `TypeError` instead of a clear Arnio API error.

## Why it matters
`normalize_unicode()` is a public cleaning helper and pipeline step candidate. Users who pass invalid configuration should receive deterministic `TypeError` / `ValueError` messages that explain the accepted values, not an implementation-level exception from set membership.

## Evidence
- `arnio/cleaning.py`: `normalize_unicode()` defines `valid_forms = {"NFC", "NFD", "NFKC", "NFKD"}` and immediately runs `if form not in valid_forms:` without first validating `form`.
- Runtime probe on current source shows `form=["NFC"]` raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Create an `ArFrame` with a string column.
2. Call `ar.normalize_unicode(frame, form=["NFC"])`.
3. Observe the raw Python exception.

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"name": ["e\u0301"]}))
ar.normalize_unicode(frame, form=["NFC"])
```

## Expected behavior
Arnio should raise a clear API-level error, for example:

```text
TypeError: form must be a string
```

or a `ValueError` that includes the supported forms when the value is a string but unsupported.

## Actual behavior
The function raises:

```text
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
```

## Suggested direction
Validate `form` before the membership check:

- reject non-string forms with `TypeError`
- keep unsupported string forms as `ValueError`
- add regression tests for valid forms, unsupported string forms, and unhashable/non-string forms

## References
- `arnio/cleaning.py`

title: Bug: reject whitespace-only DuckDB relation names
body:
## Summary
`register_duckdb()` rejects an empty relation name but accepts whitespace-only names such as `"   "` or `"\t"`. These names are effectively blank from a user/API perspective and can lead to confusing DuckDB registration behavior.

## Why it matters
Arnio's integration helpers should validate user-facing identifiers before handing data to external libraries. A whitespace-only relation name is difficult to query, debug, or document, and the current docstring already says the name must not be empty.

## Evidence
- `arnio/integrations/duckdb.py`: `register_duckdb()` checks `if not name:` but does not check `name.strip()`.
- Runtime probe with a fake DuckDB-like connection shows `""` raises `ValueError`, while `"   "` and `"\t"` are accepted and passed to `conn.register(...)`.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Create any `ArFrame`.
2. Call `register_duckdb(frame, conn, "   ")` with a DuckDB connection or DuckDB-like object.
3. The whitespace-only name is accepted.

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar
from arnio.integrations.duckdb import register_duckdb

class Conn:
    def register(self, name, df):
        print(repr(name))

frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"x": [1]}))
register_duckdb(frame, Conn(), "   ")
```

## Expected behavior
Whitespace-only names should be rejected with a clear error, for example:

```text
ValueError: name must not be empty or whitespace-only
```

## Actual behavior
Whitespace-only names are accepted and passed through to the DuckDB connection.

## Suggested direction
Update `register_duckdb()` to validate `name.strip()` before registration and add tests for:

- empty string
- whitespace-only string
- valid relation names
- non-string names

## References

title: Bug: use clear path type errors in path-only readers
body:
## Summary
Several path-based readers call `os.fspath(path)` before validating the public `path` argument, so invalid inputs receive Python's generic `os.fspath()` error instead of an Arnio-specific message.

## Why it matters
Arnio already gives a clearer path/file-like error in `read_csv()`. Keeping reader validation consistent makes the API easier to debug, especially for new contributors and users passing objects from web apps, notebooks, or CLIs.

## Evidence
- `arnio/io.py`: `sniff_delimiter()` immediately runs `path = os.fspath(path)`.
- `arnio/io.py`: `read_jsonl()` uses the same pattern.
- `arnio/io.py`: `scan_csv()` also converts with `os.fspath()` before raising a clear public error.
- Runtime probe with `path=123` produces `TypeError: expected str, bytes or os.PathLike object, not int` for `sniff_delimiter()`, `scan_csv()`, and `read_jsonl()`, while `read_csv()` raises the clearer `read_csv expected a filesystem path or text file-like object`.

## Reproduction or trigger
```python
import arnio as ar

ar.sniff_delimiter(123)
ar.scan_csv(123)
ar.read_jsonl(123)
```

## Expected behavior
Each public reader should raise a consistent Arnio-level `TypeError`, for example:

```text
scan_csv expected a filesystem path
sniff_delimiter expected a filesystem path
read_jsonl expected a filesystem path
```

## Actual behavior
The functions currently expose Python's lower-level `os.fspath()` error message.

## Suggested direction
Add a small shared path validation helper for path-only APIs, or validate `isinstance(path, (str, bytes, os.PathLike))` before calling `os.fspath()`.

Please add focused tests for invalid path types on:

- `scan_csv()`
- `sniff_delimiter()`
- `read_jsonl()`

## References
- `arnio/io.py`

title: Packaging: source distributions include arbitrary untracked workspace files
body:
## Summary
The source distribution can include local virtual-environment files when a developer has a `.venv*` directory in the repository root. In a local build, `dist/arnio-1.18.0.tar.gz` included `.venv-qa312/Lib/site-packages/pybind11/...` files.

## Why it matters
Source distributions should contain only project source and release metadata. Accidentally packaging local virtual environments can make sdists huge, leak developer-environment state, slow release builds, and make local release artifacts non-reproducible.

## Evidence
- `pyproject.toml`: there is no explicit sdist exclusion for `.venv*`, virtualenv folders, or other local build artifacts.
- Local `pipx run build --sdist` output produced `dist/arnio-1.18.0.tar.gz` containing paths such as:
  - `arnio-1.18.0/.venv-qa312/Lib/site-packages/pybind11/__init__.py`
  - `arnio-1.18.0/.venv-qa312/Lib/site-packages/pybind11/include/pybind11/pybind11.h`
  - `arnio-1.18.0/.venv-qa312/Scripts/pybind11-config.exe`
- The same archive also contains the real project files like `CMakeLists.txt`, `bindings/`, and `cpp/`, so the issue is not just an inspection false positive.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Create or keep a virtual environment directory under the repository root, for example `.venv-qa312/`.
2. Run:

```bash
pipx run build --sdist
```

3. Inspect the archive:

```bash
tar -tf dist/arnio-*.tar.gz | grep -E '^arnio-[^/]+/\.venv'
```

## Expected behavior
The sdist should exclude local virtual environments and other developer-machine artifacts.

## Actual behavior
The sdist can include `.venv*` contents from the working tree.

## Suggested direction
Add explicit sdist exclusions in the build configuration, for example using `tool.scikit-build.sdist.exclude` or an equivalent packaging mechanism. At minimum exclude:

- `.venv*`
- `venv/`
- `.tox/`
- `.mypy_cache/`
- `.pytest_cache/`
- generated local `dist/` or scratch artifacts where appropriate

Also add a release dry-run assertion that fails if the sdist contains `.venv`, `site-packages`, or other local environment paths.

## References
- `pyproject.toml`
- `.github/workflows/build_wheels.yml`

title: Bug: validate schema_to_yaml output paths before writing
body:
## Summary
`schema_to_yaml(..., path=...)` does not validate the output path before writing. Empty strings and directory paths fall through to `pathlib.Path.write_text()` and raise low-level filesystem errors instead of clear Arnio API errors.

## Why it matters
`schema_to_yaml()` is a public export helper. When users pass an invalid output target from a CLI, notebook, or config file, the error should explain that the path must be a file path, not expose a platform-specific `PermissionError` for `'.'`.

## Evidence
- `arnio/schema_export.py`: `schema_to_yaml()` converts `path` with `pathlib.Path(path)`, creates `target.parent`, and calls `target.write_text(...)` without validating whether `target` is empty, a directory, or path-like.
- Runtime probe shows:
  - `path=""` resolves to `'.'` and raises `PermissionError`
  - `path="."` raises `PermissionError`
  - non-path values such as `True` and `123` expose raw `pathlib` `TypeError` messages

## Reproduction or trigger
```python
import arnio as ar

schema = {"id": "int64"}
ar.schema_to_yaml(schema, path="")
ar.schema_to_yaml(schema, path=".")
```

## Expected behavior
Invalid output paths should fail with clear API-level errors, for example:

- `path must be a string or pathlib.Path`
- `path must not be empty`
- `path must point to a file, not a directory`

## Actual behavior
The function raises low-level `TypeError` / `PermissionError` messages from `pathlib` or the operating system.

## Suggested direction
Add output path validation before writing:

- reject non-string / non-`PathLike` values with `TypeError`
- reject empty strings with `ValueError`
- reject existing directories with `ValueError`
- keep creating parent directories for valid file paths
- add focused tests for valid file paths, empty path, directory path, and invalid path types

## References
- `arnio/schema_export.py`

nodes.body: Fixes #1674 ## Summary Add validation for `schema_to_yaml(..., path=...)` output paths before writing files. ## Changes - Reject non-string and non-`os.PathLike` values with a clear `TypeError` - Reject empty string paths with `ValueError` - Reject existing directory paths with `ValueError` - Preserve valid file-path behavior, including automatic parent directory creation - Add focused tests covering: - Valid file paths - `os.PathLike` paths - Empty string paths - Directory paths - Invalid path types - Parent directory creation ## Why Previously, invalid output paths could fall through to `pathlib.Path.write_text()` and raise low-level filesystem errors such as `PermissionError` or raw `pathlib` exceptions. This change provides clear API-level validation errors that are easier for users to understand and handle. ## Testing ```bash pytest tests/test_schema_export.py -v ``` All tests pass locally.

title: Bug: validate Field dtype values during schema construction
body:
## Summary
The public `Field` constructor accepts unsupported and non-string `dtype` values such as `"uuid"`, `123`, or `""`. These invalid field definitions are only surfaced later as confusing validation issues instead of being rejected when the schema is built.

## Why it matters
`Field` is exported as part of Arnio's public schema API. Invalid dtype contracts should fail fast at construction time so users do not run validations against impossible schema definitions.

## Evidence
- `arnio/schema.py`: `Field.__post_init__()` validates `nullable`, `unique`, numeric bounds for numeric dtypes, and severity, but does not validate `dtype` itself.
- Runtime probe shows `ar.Field(dtype=123)` and `ar.Field(dtype="uuid")` both construct successfully.
- Validation then reports messages like `expected 123` or `expected 'uuid'`, which are not valid Arnio dtypes.

## Reproduction or trigger
```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

schema = ar.Schema({"x": ar.Field(dtype=123)})
frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"x": ["a"]}))
print(ar.validate(frame, schema).to_dict())
```

## Expected behavior
`Field.__post_init__()` should reject invalid dtype values with a clear error, for example:

```text
TypeError: dtype must be a string or None
ValueError: dtype must be one of int64, float64, string, bool, datetime, or None
```

## Actual behavior
Invalid dtype values are accepted and only appear later in validation output.

## Suggested direction
Add dtype validation to `Field.__post_init__()` and test:

- valid dtypes used by Arnio
- `None`
- unsupported strings
- non-string values
- empty strings

## References
- `arnio/schema.py`

title: Bug: reject whitespace-only custom validator names
body:
## Summary
`register_validator()` accepts whitespace-only validator names such as `" "` and `"\t"`. Those names can then be used through `Custom()`, producing schema semantics like `custom: ` that are difficult to read, document, or debug.

## Why it matters
Custom validator names are part of schema contracts and serialized metadata. Whitespace-only names are effectively blank identifiers and should be rejected the same way empty strings are rejected.

## Evidence
- `arnio/schema.py`: `register_validator()` checks `if not isinstance(name, str) or not name`, but does not check `name.strip()`.
- Runtime probe shows both `ar.register_validator(" ", fn)` and `ar.register_validator("\t", fn)` succeed.
- `ar.Custom(" ")` then creates a `Field` with `semantic='custom: '`.

## Reproduction or trigger
```python
import arnio as ar

ar.register_validator(" ", lambda value: True)
field = ar.Custom(" ")
print(field.semantic)
```

## Expected behavior
Whitespace-only validator names should be rejected with a clear error, for example:

```text
ValueError: name must be a non-empty, non-whitespace string
```

## Actual behavior
Whitespace-only names are accepted and become part of the schema semantic string.

## Suggested direction
Update `register_validator()` to reject `not name.strip()` and add tests for:

- empty names
- whitespace-only names
- valid names
- non-string names

## References
- `arnio/schema.py`

title: Bug: validate ArnioCleaner steps configuration before transform
body:
## Summary

`ArnioCleaner` accepts invalid `steps` values such as a bare string during construction, but the failure only appears later during `fit_transform()` after the string has been iterated character-by-character.

## Why it matters

`ArnioCleaner` is a scikit-learn estimator, so users configure it through constructor arguments, `Pipeline`, and `set_params()`. Invalid pipeline configuration should fail with a clear estimator-level message instead of surfacing as `Invalid step format: 's'` from the lower-level pipeline executor.

## Evidence

- `arnio/integrations/sklearn.py`: `ArnioCleaner.__init__()` stores `self.steps = steps if steps is not None else []` without validating the shape.
- `arnio/integrations/sklearn.py`: `transform()` passes `self.steps` directly to `arnio.pipeline.pipeline()`.
- `arnio/pipeline.py`: `_validate_pipeline_steps()` iterates `steps`, so a bare string is treated as individual characters.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
from arnio.integrations.sklearn import ArnioCleaner

cleaner = ArnioCleaner(steps="strip_whitespace")
cleaner.fit_transform(pd.DataFrame({"a": [" x "]}))
```

## Expected behavior

`ArnioCleaner` should reject invalid `steps` values with a clear `TypeError` or `ValueError`, for example explaining that `steps` must be a list/tuple of pipeline step tuples.

## Actual behavior

The constructor accepts the string, and transform later fails with a confusing lower-level message such as:

```text
Invalid step format: 's'. Expected (name,) or (name, kwargs)
```

## Suggested direction

Add an internal `steps` validation helper for `ArnioCleaner` and call it from `__init__()` and from `fit()`/`transform()` so `set_params(steps=...)` is also validated. Add tests for:

- bare string `steps`
- mapping/dict `steps`
- non-tuple entries inside the sequence
- valid step lists continuing to work

## References

- `arnio/integrations/sklearn.py::ArnioCleaner`
- `arnio/pipeline.py::_validate_pipeline_steps`

title: Bug: validate Email schema validation mode type
body:
## Summary

`ar.Email(validation=...)` does not validate the type of `validation` before checking membership in the allowed modes. Passing an unhashable value such as a list leaks a raw Python `TypeError` instead of Arnio's intended schema configuration message.

## Why it matters

Schema factories are public user-facing APIs. Configuration mistakes should fail early with clear, actionable errors, especially for GSSoC contributors and users building production validation contracts.

## Evidence

- `arnio/schema.py`: `Email()` checks `if validation not in {"light", "strict"}` directly.
- That membership check assumes `validation` is hashable.
- Existing tests cover invalid values like unsupported modes, but not unhashable values.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import arnio as ar

ar.Email(validation=["light"])
```

## Expected behavior

The factory should raise a clear error such as:

```text
TypeError: Email validation must be a string: 'light' or 'strict'
```

or a clear `ValueError` explaining the accepted modes.

## Actual behavior

Python raises a raw implementation detail:

```text
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
```

## Suggested direction

Validate `validation` before the membership check:

- reject non-string values with a clear `TypeError`
- keep rejecting unsupported string values with `ValueError`
- add tests for list, set, `None`, unsupported strings, and valid modes

## References

- `tests/test_schema.py`

title: Bug: reject empty file_path in DataQualityReport.to_html
body:
## Summary

`DataQualityReport.to_html(file_path="")` silently behaves like `file_path=None`: it returns the HTML string and does not write a file, even though the caller explicitly provided a path value.

## Why it matters

Report-export APIs should fail clearly on invalid output paths. Treating an empty string as “no output path” can hide configuration bugs in notebooks, CLI wrappers, or CI jobs that expect a report artifact to be written.

## Evidence

- `arnio/quality.py`: `DataQualityReport.to_html()` validates the type when `file_path is not None`, but later writes only inside `if file_path:`.
- Because `""` is falsy, the function skips file writing and returns HTML instead of raising a path validation error.
- Similar path validation issues are already handled in other public exports, such as `schema_to_yaml()`.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
from arnio.quality import DataQualityReport

report = DataQualityReport(
    row_count=0,
    column_count=0,
    memory_usage=0,
    duplicate_rows=0,
    duplicate_ratio=0,
    columns={},
)

html = report.to_html(file_path="")
print(type(html).__name__)
```

## Expected behavior

Passing an empty string as `file_path` should raise a clear `ValueError`, for example `file_path must not be empty`.

## Actual behavior

The empty path is silently ignored and the method returns the HTML string as if no output path had been supplied.

## Suggested direction

- Add explicit empty-string/path validation after type validation.
- Change the write branch from truthiness-based `if file_path:` to `if file_path is not None:` after validation.
- Add tests for `file_path=""` and valid string/path-like output paths.

## References

- `arnio/quality.py::DataQualityReport.to_html`
- `tests/test_quality.py`

body:
## Summary

`Schema.to_json()` can crash when a field's `allowed` set contains mixed scalar types, because the serializer tries to sort the set directly.

## Why it matters

`String(allowed=...)` is typed as accepting `Any` values, and mixed scalar allow-lists can be valid for messy CSV validation. Serialization should either preserve those schemas safely or reject them at construction time with a clear error. A raw sort comparison error makes schema export unreliable.

## Evidence

- `arnio/schema.py`: `_normalize_sequence()` converts sets with `sorted(value)`.
- Python cannot sort sets containing incomparable types such as `int` and `str`.
- `Schema.to_json()` calls `_field_to_json_dict()`, which eventually normalizes `field_def.allowed` through this helper.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import arnio as ar

schema = ar.Schema({
    "code": ar.String(allowed={1, "1"}),
})

schema.to_json()
```

## Expected behavior

Schema serialization should produce stable JSON for supported allowed values, or schema construction should reject mixed-type allowed values with a clear error.

## Actual behavior

`Schema.to_json()` raises a raw Python sorting error:

```text
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'
```

## Suggested direction

Use a JSON-safe deterministic ordering strategy that does not compare raw mixed types, for example sorting by `(type(value).__name__, repr(value))`, or explicitly validate allowed values to a narrower supported type set. Add tests for:

- homogeneous string allowed values
- homogeneous numeric allowed values
- mixed scalar allowed values
- round-tripping through `Schema.to_json()` / `Schema.from_json()`

## References

- `arnio/schema.py::_normalize_sequence`
- `arnio/schema.py::Schema.to_json`
- `tests/test_schema.py`
- `tests/test_schema_export.py`

nodes.title: fix: deterministic sort for mixed-type allowed values
nodes.body:
Fixes #1682

`_normalize_sequence()` called `sorted(value)` directly on sets, which raises `TypeError` when the set contains mixed scalar types like `{1, "1"}` since Python can't compare `int` and `str` with `<`.

Replaced with a type-safe key:

```python
sorted(value, key=lambda x: (type(x).__name__, repr(x)))
```

Tests added for homogeneous strings, homogeneous numerics, mixed scalars, and `to_json()` / `from_json()` round-trip.

title: Bug: add Frame.select_rows to native type stubs
body:
## Summary

The native extension stub `arnio/_arnio_cpp.pyi` is missing the `Frame.select_rows()` method, even though the method is bound in pybind11 and used by `ArFrame.head()` / `ArFrame.tail()`.

## Why it matters

Arnio ships `py.typed`, so type checkers and IDEs rely on the stub files. Missing native methods make valid internal and user-facing code appear broken, and they reduce confidence in Arnio's typed API.

## Evidence

- `bindings/bind_arnio.cpp`: binds `.def("select_rows", &Frame::select_rows)`.
- `arnio/frame.py`: `ArFrame.head()` calls `self._frame.select_rows(0, actual_n)`.
- `arnio/frame.py`: `ArFrame.tail()` calls `self._frame.select_rows(start, actual_n)`.
- `arnio/_arnio_cpp.pyi`: `class Frame` lists methods such as `select_columns()` and `clone()`, but not `select_rows()`.

## Reproduction or trigger

1. Run a type checker over `arnio/frame.py` using the shipped stubs.
2. Inspect the `Frame` stub in `arnio/_arnio_cpp.pyi`.
3. `select_rows` is missing even though the method exists at runtime.

## Expected behavior

`Frame.select_rows(start: int, count: int) -> Frame` should be present in `_arnio_cpp.pyi` and match the native binding signature.

## Actual behavior

The stub omits the method, so typed consumers cannot see the API that `ArFrame.head()` and `ArFrame.tail()` depend on.

## Suggested direction

- Add `def select_rows(self, start: int, count: int) -> Frame: ...` to `arnio/_arnio_cpp.pyi`.
- Add or update a type-checking test if the project has one for native stubs.
- Verify that `ArFrame.head()` and `ArFrame.tail()` continue to type-check.

## References

- `arnio/_arnio_cpp.pyi`
- `bindings/bind_arnio.cpp`
- `arnio/frame.py`

nodes.body: Fixes #1683. Adds the missing select_rows method signature to the Frame class in the native stub file _arnio_cpp.pyi.

title: Bug: validate ValidationResult constructor fields
body:
## Summary
`ValidationResult` is exported as part of the public schema API, but its constructor accepts invalid or inconsistent values. Invalid `issues`, `bad_rows`, `row_count`, and `issue_count` values can later produce misleading summaries or crash during serialization.

## Why it matters
Users can create validation results in tests, custom validators, notebooks, or docs examples. A public result object should fail early with a clear error instead of storing invalid state and failing later in `passed`, `summary()`, `to_dict()`, or `to_markdown()`.

## Evidence
- `arnio/schema.py`: `ValidationResult` is a frozen dataclass with no `__post_init__` validation.
- `arnio/__init__.py`: `ValidationResult` is exported in `__all__`.
- `ValidationResult(row_count="1", issue_count=0, issues=[]).to_dict()` returns `row_count` as a string.
- `ValidationResult(row_count=1, issue_count=1, issues=["bad"]).to_dict()` raises `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'severity'`.
- `ValidationResult(row_count=1, issue_count=0, issues=[], bad_rows="abc").summary()` reports `bad_row_count` as `3` because the string is treated as an iterable.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Run:
   ```python
   import arnio as ar

   ar.ValidationResult(row_count="1", issue_count=0, issues=[]).to_dict()
   ar.ValidationResult(row_count=1, issue_count=1, issues=["bad"]).to_dict()
   ar.ValidationResult(row_count=1, issue_count=0, issues=[], bad_rows="abc").summary()
   ```
2. Observe invalid serialized output or raw `AttributeError` failures.

## Expected behavior
`ValidationResult` should validate constructor inputs and reject invalid state with clear `TypeError` or `ValueError` messages.

## Actual behavior
Invalid values are accepted and later either serialize incorrectly or crash in downstream methods.

## Suggested direction
- Add `ValidationResult.__post_init__` validation.
- Require `row_count` and `issue_count` to be non-negative integers.
- Require `issues` to be a list of `ValidationIssue` instances.
- Require `bad_rows` to be a list of non-negative integers.
- Consider validating `issue_count == len(issues)` or documenting when they can intentionally differ due truncation.
- Add focused tests in `tests/test_schema.py`.

## References
- `arnio/schema.py`
- `arnio/__init__.py`
- Related existing issue: #1667 covers `ValidationIssue`, but not `ValidationResult`.

title: Bug: validate QualityGateResult constructor fields
body:
## Summary
`QualityGateIssue` and `QualityGateResult` are exported public quality-reporting objects, but they do not validate their constructor inputs. Invalid issue objects, profiles, or threshold values can crash during serialization or expose malformed dictionaries.

## Why it matters
Quality gates are meant for CI and release checks. If users construct or manipulate these objects directly, invalid state should be rejected immediately with clear validation errors instead of failing later in automation.

## Evidence
- `arnio/quality.py`: `QualityGateIssue` and `QualityGateResult` are dataclasses with no constructor validation.
- `arnio/__init__.py`: both classes are exported in `__all__`.
- `QualityGateIssue(metric=1, message=2, column=3).to_dict()` returns non-string fields directly.
- `QualityGateResult(None, None, ["bad"], {}).to_dict()` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'row_count'`.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Run:
   ```python
   import arnio as ar

   ar.QualityGateIssue(metric=1, message=2, column=3).to_dict()
   ar.QualityGateResult(None, None, ["bad"], {}).to_dict()
   ```
2. Observe malformed serialized output or raw `AttributeError`.

## Expected behavior
Quality gate result objects should validate their public fields and raise clear `TypeError`/`ValueError` messages for invalid inputs.

## Actual behavior
Invalid values are accepted and fail later in export/reporting methods.

## Suggested direction
- Add `__post_init__` validation to `QualityGateIssue` and `QualityGateResult`.
- Require `metric` and `message` to be non-empty strings.
- Require `column` to be `str | None`.
- Require `delta` to be numeric or `None`.
- Require `baseline_profile` and `current_profile` to be `DataQualityReport` instances.
- Require `issues` to be a list of `QualityGateIssue` instances.
- Require `thresholds` to be a dictionary.
- Add focused tests in `tests/test_quality.py`.

## References
- `arnio/quality.py`
- `tests/test_quality.py`

title: Bug: validate CleanExplanation result object fields
body:
## Summary
`CleanStepRecord` and `CleanExplanation` are exported public objects for `auto_clean(explain=True)`, but they do not validate their constructor inputs. Invalid records can crash `CleanExplanation.__str__()` or produce misleading explain output.

## Why it matters
Explain-mode output is intended to be a trustworthy audit trail for automatic cleaning. If these public objects are constructed in tests, docs, or integrations, invalid state should fail clearly instead of creating broken reports.

## Evidence
- `arnio/quality.py`: `CleanStepRecord` and `CleanExplanation` are dataclasses without validation.
- `arnio/__init__.py`: both classes are exported in `__all__`.
- `str(CleanExplanation(mode=123, rows_before="a", rows_after=None, rows_removed=[], steps=["bad"]))` raises `AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'step'`.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Run:
   ```python
   import arnio as ar

   explanation = ar.CleanExplanation(
       mode=123,
       rows_before="a",
       rows_after=None,
       rows_removed=[],
       steps=["bad"],
   )
   str(explanation)
   ```
2. Observe a raw `AttributeError` from the string renderer.

## Expected behavior
`CleanStepRecord` and `CleanExplanation` should validate their public fields and reject invalid state at construction time.

## Actual behavior
Invalid state is accepted and only fails later when rendering or consuming the explanation.

## Suggested direction
- Add `__post_init__` validation to both dataclasses.
- Require `mode`, `step`, and `reason` to be strings.
- Require `kwargs` to be a dict.
- Require row counts and rows removed to be non-negative integers.
- Require `steps` to be a list of `CleanStepRecord` instances.
- Add regression tests around `auto_clean(explain=True)` result objects and invalid constructors.

## References
- `arnio/quality.py`
- `tests/test_quality.py`

title: Bug: validate writer output path arguments
body:
## Summary
`write_csv()` and `write_parquet()` convert their output path with `os.fspath(path)` before validating the public path argument. Invalid path values such as `True` or arbitrary objects currently surface Python's low-level `os.fspath()` error instead of an Arnio-specific writer error.

## Why it matters
Writer APIs are commonly used in notebooks, scripts, and CI jobs. A clear validation message helps users distinguish invalid output-path input from writer/backend failures.

## Evidence
- `arnio/io.py`: `write_csv()` calls `path = os.fspath(path)` before any path-type validation.
- `arnio/io.py`: `write_parquet()` does the same before extension/compression validation.
- Existing issue #1408 covers invalid `frame` inputs for writers, but not invalid writer output paths.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Run:
   ```python
   import arnio as ar
   import pandas as pd

   frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1]}))
   ar.write_csv(frame, True)
   ar.write_parquet(frame, True)
   ```
2. Observe raw `TypeError: expected str, bytes or os.PathLike object, not bool` from `os.fspath()`.

## Expected behavior
Writers should reject invalid output paths with a clear public API error, for example `TypeError: path must be a string, bytes, or os.PathLike object`.

## Actual behavior
The raw `os.fspath()` error leaks through before Arnio can explain which argument is invalid.

## Suggested direction
- Add a small path validator for writer output paths.
- Explicitly reject booleans.
- Keep valid `str`, `bytes`, and `os.PathLike` behavior unchanged.
- Add tests for invalid `path` values in `tests/test_write_csv.py` and `tests/test_parquet.py`.

## References
- `arnio/io.py`
- `tests/test_write_csv.py`
- `tests/test_parquet.py`
- Related issue: #1408 covers writer `frame` validation.

title: Bug: profile non-finite numeric values without runtime warnings
body:
## Summary
`profile()` filters non-finite numeric values before building histograms, but it still computes `min`, `max`, `mean`, `std`, and quantiles on the unfiltered numeric series. Columns containing `inf` or `-inf` therefore emit NumPy `RuntimeWarning`s and produce `nan`/`inf` summary stats even though the histogram intentionally ignores those values.

## Why it matters
Quality reports are often used in notebooks and CI. Runtime warnings and non-finite summary statistics make reports noisy and harder to trust, especially when Arnio already has logic to handle finite values safely for histograms.

## Evidence
- `arnio/quality.py`: `_profile_column()` computes numeric stats from `numeric_non_null` before creating `finite_values = numeric_non_null[np.isfinite(numeric_non_null)]` for the histogram.
- `tests/test_quality.py`: `test_profile_numeric_histogram_non_finite_values` verifies histogram behavior for infinities, but it does not assert that warnings are suppressed or that numeric summary stats are finite.
- Runtime probe on current source emits `RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in reduce` and returns `mean=nan`, `std=nan`, `min=-inf`, `max=inf`.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Run:
   ```python
   import warnings
   import arnio as ar
   from arnio._core import _DType, _Frame
   from arnio.frame import ArFrame

   frame = ArFrame(_Frame.from_dict(
       {"nums": [1.0, 2.0, float("inf"), float("-inf"), None, 3.0]},
       {"nums": _DType.FLOAT64},
   ))

   with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
       warnings.simplefilter("always")
       prof = ar.profile(frame).columns["nums"]

   print([str(w.message) for w in caught])
   print(prof.min, prof.max, prof.mean, prof.std, prof.q75, prof.q95)
   ```
2. Observe runtime warnings and non-finite stats.

## Expected behavior
Numeric profiling should handle non-finite values consistently: either exclude them from all numeric stats or document/report them separately without emitting runtime warnings.

## Actual behavior
Only the histogram uses the finite subset. Other numeric stats are computed on `inf`/`-inf`, causing warnings and `nan`/`inf` values in the report.

## Suggested direction
- Compute numeric summary stats from finite numeric values when any finite values exist.
- Keep `histogram=None` when no finite values exist.
- Consider adding a warning/count field for non-finite values if the report needs to expose that data-quality signal.
- Add tests that assert `profile()` does not emit `RuntimeWarning` for `inf`/`-inf` columns and that finite stats remain stable.

## References
- `arnio/quality.py`
- `tests/test_quality.py`

nodes.title: Fix: Profile for non-finite numeric values without runtime warnings
nodes.body: ## Summary This PR fixes numeric profiling for columns containing non-finite values (`inf`, `-inf`, `NaN`). Previously, `profile()` filtered non-finite values only when generating histograms, while numeric summary statistics (`min`, `max`, `mean`, `std`, `q25`, `q50`, `q75`, `q95`) were still computed on the unfiltered series. This could emit NumPy `RuntimeWarnings` and produce `NaN`/`Infinity` values in quality reports. The fix computes all numeric summary statistics using only finite values. When a column contains no finite values, numeric statistics are set to `None` and `histogram=None` is returned. This removes runtime warnings, keeps profiling behavior consistent, and prevents non-finite summary statistics from appearing in serialized reports. `tests/test_quality.py` was updated to verify that: - Profiling columns containing inf/-inf emits no RuntimeWarnings. - Histograms continue to ignore non-finite values. - Numeric statistics remain finite when finite values are present. - Columns containing only non-finite values are handled safely. - Generated reports remain valid for strict JSON serialization. ## Linked issue Fixes #1690 ## Type of change - [x] Bug fix - [ ] Feature - [ ] Performance improvement - [ ] Documentation - [x] Tests - [ ] Refactor - [ ] CI / packaging ## Area - [ ] CSV parser / I/O - [ ] C++ cleaning engine - [ ] Python API / ArFrame - [ ] Pipeline / custom steps - [x] Data quality / profiling - [ ] Schema validation - [ ] pandas interoperability - [ ] Docs / website - [ ] Developer tooling ## Testing ```powershell pytest tests/test_quality.py -v ``` - [x] `make test` (or `python -m pytest tests -v --cov=arnio`) - [x] `make lint` (or run separately: ```powershell python -m ruff check . python -m black --check . ``` ) - [ ] optionally `python -m pytest tests -v --tb=short -x` - [ ] Other: ## Contributor checklist - [x] I read the contributing guide. - [x] I kept the PR focused on one issue or one logical change. - [x] I added or updated tests for behavior changes. - [ ] I added or updated docs/examples for public API changes. - [x] I checked that generated files, logs, and local build artifacts are not committed. - [x] My PR title uses Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `test:`, `refactor:`, `chore:`).

title: Bug: bound quality gate ratio thresholds to valid ratio ranges
body:
## Summary
`check_quality_gates()` validates drift thresholds as finite non-negative numbers, but ratio-delta gates such as `max_duplicate_ratio_delta` and `max_null_ratio_delta` also accept values greater than `1.0`.

## Why it matters
Duplicate ratio and null ratio deltas are absolute differences between ratios, so their meaningful range is `0.0` to `1.0`. Accepting values such as `1.5` silently weakens the gate and can hide real data-quality regressions in CI or release checks.

## Evidence
- `arnio/quality.py`: `check_quality_gates()` documents `max_duplicate_ratio_delta` and `max_null_ratio_delta` as maximum absolute ratio drift thresholds.
- `arnio/quality.py`: `_validate_gate_threshold()` only checks for finite non-negative numbers, not whether ratio thresholds are bounded to the valid ratio range.
- Runtime probe on current `origin/main` accepted `max_duplicate_ratio_delta=1.5` and `max_null_ratio_delta=1.5` without error.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Create two simple profiles:
   ```python
   import pandas as pd
   import arnio as ar

   frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3]}))
   report = ar.profile(frame)
   ```
2. Run:
   ```python
   ar.check_quality_gates(report, report, max_duplicate_ratio_delta=1.5)
   ar.check_quality_gates(report, report, max_null_ratio_delta=1.5)
   ```

## Expected behavior
Ratio-delta thresholds should reject values outside `0.0 <= threshold <= 1.0`, or the docs should explicitly explain why values above `1.0` are allowed.

## Actual behavior
The calls succeed and store impossible ratio thresholds in the returned `QualityGateResult.thresholds` mapping.

## Suggested direction
Add a small ratio-threshold validator for absolute ratio gates. Keep relative numeric gates such as mean/std delta separate because values above `1.0` may be meaningful there.

## References
- `arnio/quality.py`
- `tests/test_quality.py`

nodes.title: fix: bound quality gate ratio thresholds to valid ratio ranges
nodes.body:
## Summary
Enforced an upper bound of 1.0 on absolute data quality ratio gates. 

Previously, `check_quality_gates()` allowed absolute ratio differences like `max_duplicate_ratio_delta` and `max_null_ratio_delta` to accept values greater than 1.0 (e.g., 1.5). Because absolute proportions are strictly bounded between 0.0 and 1.0, these settings silently weakened quality gates in CI and execution tests. 

Introduced a private helper validator `_validate_gate_ratio_threshold` to properly enforce the `[0.0, 1.0]` constraint while preserving normal scale validation for relative gates like numeric mean/std metrics.

title: Bug: reject NaN approx_top_values_min_ratio in profile()
body:
## Summary
`profile()` accepts `approx_top_values_min_ratio=float("nan")` even though the option is documented and validated as a ratio between `0` and `1`.

## Why it matters
`NaN` comparisons are always false, so the existing `value < 0 or value > 1` check lets `NaN` through. That makes approximate-top-value behavior harder to reason about and can silently disable or distort profiling heuristics.

## Evidence
- `arnio/quality.py`: `profile()` validates `approx_top_values_min_ratio` with lower/upper comparisons but does not check `math.isfinite()`.
- Runtime probe on current `origin/main`:
  ```python
  import math
  import pandas as pd
  import arnio as ar

  frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"x": ["a", "b"]}))
  report = ar.profile(frame, approx_top_values=True, approx_top_values_min_ratio=math.nan)
  ```
  The call succeeds instead of rejecting the invalid ratio.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Build a small string frame.
2. Call `ar.profile(frame, approx_top_values=True, approx_top_values_min_ratio=float("nan"))`.

## Expected behavior
Raise `ValueError` explaining that `approx_top_values_min_ratio` must be a finite ratio between `0` and `1`.

## Actual behavior
The call succeeds and carries on with `NaN` comparison semantics.

## Suggested direction
Use `math.isfinite()` or equivalent validation after the numeric type check, then keep the existing `0 <= value <= 1` bounds.

## References
- `arnio/quality.py`
- `tests/test_quality.py`

title: Bug: validate ArFrame.astype dtype arguments before pandas casting
body:
## Summary
`ArFrame.astype()` does not validate the `dtype` argument before delegating to pandas. Some invalid dtype inputs leak through pandas and fail later during conversion back to `ArFrame` with confusing, unrelated errors.

## Why it matters
`astype()` is now a public convenience wrapper. Invalid dtype configuration should fail at the API boundary with a clear message, especially because this helper is intended to feel familiar to pandas users while still preserving Arnio's stricter runtime contracts.

## Evidence
- `arnio/frame.py`: `ArFrame.astype()` only rejects `dtype is None`, then runs `df.astype(dtype)` and converts the result back with `from_pandas()`.
- Runtime probe on current `origin/main`:
  ```python
  import pandas as pd
  import arnio as ar

  frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": ["x", "y"]}))
  frame.astype([])
  ```
  This raises:
  ```text
  TypeError: Column 'a' contains unsupported nested value of type 'tuple' at value (). Convert nested objects to strings or flatten them first.
  ```
  The actual problem is an invalid dtype argument, not nested source data.

## Reproduction or trigger
1. Create an `ArFrame` from a simple pandas DataFrame.
2. Call `frame.astype([])` or another unsupported dtype container.
3. Observe that the failure happens after pandas conversion rather than at dtype validation.

## Expected behavior
`ArFrame.astype()` should reject unsupported dtype argument shapes directly, for example with:

```text
TypeError: dtype must be a string, Python type, NumPy/pandas dtype, or mapping of column names to dtypes
```

## Actual behavior
The invalid dtype value reaches pandas and may produce transformed data that fails later in `from_pandas()` with an unrelated nested-value error.

## Suggested direction
- Validate accepted dtype argument shapes before calling `DataFrame.astype()`.
- For mapping inputs, validate that keys are existing column names before casting.
- Add tests for invalid containers, missing mapping keys, valid scalar dtype, and valid mapping dtype.

## References
- `arnio/frame.py`
- `tests/test_frame.py`
- Original feature issue: #223

title: Bug: reject unknown keys in Schema.from_json payloads
body:
## Summary

`Schema.from_json()` silently ignores unknown keys in schema JSON payloads. This happens both at the top level and inside each field definition. For example, `uniqe` is ignored instead of being rejected, and `nulllable` inside a field falls back to the default `nullable=True` behavior.

## Why it matters

Schema JSON is likely to be used in CI and data-contract workflows. Silently ignoring misspelled keys can weaken validation without any visible failure, which is risky for production data-quality gates.

## Evidence

- `arnio/schema.py`: `Schema.from_json()` reads known top-level keys with `payload.get(...)` and ignores unknown keys.
- `arnio/schema.py`: `_field_from_json_dict()` reads known field keys with `payload.get(...)` but does not reject unknown field keys.
- Current behavior accepts typoed keys and discards them.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import json
import arnio as ar

schema = ar.Schema.from_json(json.dumps({
    "fields": {
        "email": {
            "dtype": "string",
            "nulllable": False
        }
    },
    "strict": False,
    "uniqe": ["email"]
}))

print(schema.fields["email"].nullable)  # True because the typo was ignored
print(schema.unique)                     # None because the typo was ignored
```

## Expected behavior

`Schema.from_json()` should raise a clear `ValueError` or `TypeError` for unknown schema JSON keys, ideally listing unsupported keys and allowed keys at the relevant level.

## Actual behavior

Unknown keys are ignored and defaults are used silently.

## Suggested direction

Add allowlists for supported top-level schema keys and supported field payload keys. Reject unknown keys before constructing `Schema` or `Field`. Keep `rules_omitted` accepted because it is intentionally emitted by `Schema.to_json()`.

Add tests for:

- unknown top-level key such as `uniqe`
- unknown field key such as `nulllable`
- valid payloads generated by `Schema.to_json()`

## References

- `arnio/schema.py`
- `tests/test_schema.py`

title: Bug: reject duplicate columns in Schema unique constraints
body:
## Summary

`Schema(unique=...)` accepts duplicate column names such as `unique=["id", "id"]`. The validator then runs a composite uniqueness check with repeated subset entries and reports messages like `Duplicate rows found for columns ['id', 'id']`.

## Why it matters

Composite uniqueness rules are schema contracts. Duplicate column names in the contract are almost always a configuration mistake, and accepting them makes validation output confusing for users and CI logs.

## Evidence

- `arnio/schema.py`: `Schema.__post_init__()` validates that `unique` is a list/tuple of strings, but does not check for duplicate names.
- `arnio/schema.py`: `validate()` passes `list(schema.unique)` directly to `df.duplicated(...)`.
- Runtime behavior accepts repeated names and reports the repeated list in validation messages.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1]}))
schema = ar.Schema({"id": ar.Int64()}, unique=["id", "id"])
result = ar.validate(frame, schema)

print(result.issues[0].message)
```

## Expected behavior

`Schema(unique=...)` should reject duplicate names early with a clear `ValueError`, for example `Schema 'unique' must not contain duplicate column names`.

## Actual behavior

The duplicated list is accepted and validation produces confusing `composite_unique` messages.

## Suggested direction

Add duplicate-name validation in `Schema.__post_init__()` after type checking `unique`. Add tests for direct construction and JSON deserialization via `Schema.from_json()`.

## References

- `arnio/schema.py`
- `tests/test_schema.py`

title: Bug: validate ProfileComparison constructor fields
body:
## Summary

`ProfileComparison` is exported as part of Arnio's public quality API, but its constructor does not validate its field types. Invalid profiles or drift payloads are accepted and then fail later during serialization with raw attribute errors.

## Why it matters

Profile comparison is intended for drift reporting and CI-style quality checks. Invalid comparison objects should fail at construction with clear messages, not later when a report is being serialized or written into automation logs.

## Evidence

- `arnio/quality.py`: `ProfileComparison` is a dataclass with no `__post_init__` validation.
- `arnio/__init__.py`: `ProfileComparison` is exported in `__all__`.
- `ProfileComparison.to_dict()` assumes `left_profile` and `right_profile` expose `to_dict()`.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import arnio as ar

comparison = ar.ProfileComparison(
    left_profile={},
    right_profile={},
    drift_report=[],
)
comparison.to_dict()
```

## Expected behavior

Constructing an invalid `ProfileComparison` should raise a clear `TypeError` or `ValueError`, for example when profiles are not `DataQualityReport` instances or `drift_report` is not a dictionary.

## Actual behavior

The object is constructed successfully and later raises `AttributeError: 'dict' object has no attribute 'to_dict'` during serialization.

## Suggested direction

Add `__post_init__` validation for:

- `left_profile` and `right_profile` as `DataQualityReport`
- `drift_report` as `dict[str, dict[str, Any]]`
- `status_counts` as `dict[str, int]`

Add focused tests in `tests/test_quality.py` for invalid profiles, invalid drift report shape, invalid status counts, and one valid comparison object.

## References

- `arnio/quality.py`
- `tests/test_quality.py`

title: Bug: validate required_if expected values as scalars
body:
## Summary

`required_if` accepts non-scalar expected values, but validation later compares the full condition column against that object. Values such as lists, tuples, or dictionaries can raise raw pandas errors instead of a clear schema validation error.

## Why it matters

Conditional required fields are part of Arnio's schema contract system. Invalid rule configuration should fail when the field is created or when the schema is built, not during data validation with pandas-specific exceptions.

## Evidence

- `arnio/schema.py`: `Field.__post_init__()` validates that `required_if` is a 2-item tuple and that the first item is a string.
- `arnio/schema.py`: `_validate_column()` later executes `df[condition_column] == expected_value` without validating that `expected_value` is a scalar.
- Non-scalar expected values can raise `ValueError` or `NotImplementedError` from pandas comparison internals.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({
    "flag": ["yes", "no"],
    "value": [None, None],
}))

schema = {
    "value": ar.String(required_if=("flag", ["yes"]))
}

ar.validate(frame, schema)
```

## Expected behavior

`required_if` should reject non-scalar expected values with a clear `TypeError`, or document and implement collection matching intentionally.

## Actual behavior

Validation raises a raw pandas error such as `ValueError: Lengths must match to compare`.

## Suggested direction

Use `pandas.api.types.is_scalar()` or equivalent validation in `Field.__post_init__()` for `required_if[1]`. Add tests for list, tuple, dict, and a valid scalar expected value.

## References

- `arnio/schema.py`
- `tests/test_schema.py`

title: Bug: reject invalid URL allowed_schemes values
body:
## Summary

`URL(allowed_schemes=...)` accepts invalid scheme strings such as `"https://"`, `"https ftp"`, or values starting with a digit. Those values are stored in the semantic rule and later produce confusing validation behavior.

## Why it matters

`allowed_schemes` is a schema contract option. Invalid scheme configuration should fail early with a clear message instead of creating a field that cannot validate URLs as intended.

## Evidence

- `arnio/schema.py`: `URL()` checks that each scheme is a non-empty string, then escapes it into the semantic value.
- There is no validation that scheme names match a URL scheme shape, such as starting with a letter and containing only letters, digits, `+`, `.`, or `-`.
- Current runtime accepts invalid scheme strings.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import arnio as ar

print(ar.URL(allowed_schemes=["https://"]))
print(ar.URL(allowed_schemes=["https ftp"]))
print(ar.URL(allowed_schemes=["1http"]))
```

## Expected behavior

Invalid scheme names should raise a clear `ValueError`, for example `allowed_schemes must contain URL scheme names such as 'http' or 'https'`.

## Actual behavior

The invalid strings are accepted and stored in the field semantic rule.

## Suggested direction

Validate each scheme with a small regex such as `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9+.-]*$`, normalize case if #1699 is addressed, and add focused tests for invalid scheme strings.

## References

- `arnio/schema.py`
- `tests/test_schema.py`
- Related: #1699

title: Bug: make drop_columns_matching handle zero-column frames
body:
## Summary

`drop_columns_matching()` raises `ValueError("Pattern matches all columns...")` for zero-column frames, even when the regex matches nothing. This affects both pandas DataFrames with no columns and Arnio zero-column frames.

## Why it matters

Zero-column frames can appear after column-selection or cleaning workflows, especially when users preserve row counts separately. A no-op regex drop on an already zero-column frame should not be reported as a dangerous all-column drop.

## Evidence

- `arnio/cleaning.py`: `drop_columns_matching()` computes `cols_to_drop`, then raises when `len(cols_to_drop) == len(df.columns)`.
- When `df.columns` is empty, both lengths are `0`, so the all-columns guard fires even though no column matched.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

empty_columns = pd.DataFrame(index=range(2))
ar.drop_columns_matching(empty_columns, "^tmp")
```

The same behavior occurs after converting the zero-column pandas frame with `ar.from_pandas(...)`.

## Expected behavior

When there are zero columns and the pattern matches zero columns, the function should return the frame unchanged or raise a clearer zero-column-specific error if zero-column input is intentionally unsupported.

## Actual behavior

The function raises `ValueError: Pattern matches all columns. At least one column must remain.` even though there are no columns to match.

## Suggested direction

Handle zero-column frames before the all-columns guard, or change the guard to require at least one column before treating the match as an all-column drop. Add tests for zero-column pandas and ArFrame inputs.

## References

- `arnio/cleaning.py`
- `tests/test_cleaning.py`

title: Bug: reject duplicate subset columns in multi-column helpers
body:
## Summary

Some multi-column cleaning helpers accept duplicate names in `subset`. For `combine_columns()`, this changes the output by joining the same column multiple times, for example `subset=["a", "a"]` produces `"x x"`.

## Why it matters

A duplicated subset is almost always a configuration mistake. Arnio already rejects duplicate names in `ArFrame.select_columns()`, so multi-column cleaning helpers should behave consistently and fail clearly instead of silently using the same column twice.

## Evidence

- `arnio/cleaning.py`: `_validate_existing_column_sequence()` validates types and existence, but does not reject duplicate names.
- `arnio/cleaning.py`: `combine_columns()` uses the returned `subset_columns` directly when joining values.
- `arnio/cleaning.py`: `coalesce_columns()` also accepts duplicate subset names, hiding a likely configuration mistake.
- `arnio/frame.py`: `ArFrame.select_columns()` already rejects duplicate column names, showing the stricter behavior exists elsewhere.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"a": ["x"], "b": ["y"]}))
result = ar.combine_columns(frame, subset=["a", "a"], output_column="combined")
print(ar.to_pandas(result)["combined"].tolist())
```

## Expected behavior

Helpers that consume a column subset should reject duplicate subset entries with a clear `ValueError` unless duplicate usage is intentionally supported and documented.

## Actual behavior

`combine_columns()` silently uses the same column twice and produces `"x x"`.

## Suggested direction

Add optional duplicate rejection to the shared column-sequence validator or add helper-specific checks in `combine_columns()` and `coalesce_columns()`. Add tests for duplicate subset entries in both direct and pipeline usage.

## References

- `arnio/cleaning.py`
- `arnio/frame.py`
- `tests/test_cleaning.py`

title: Bug: report column length mismatches in from_dict
body:
## Summary

`arnio.from_dict()` delegates unequal column lengths directly to pandas, which raises `ValueError: All arrays must be of the same length`. Arnio does not validate the lengths itself or identify which columns are mismatched.

## Why it matters

`from_dict()` is a public constructor. When users build frames from dictionaries, length mismatch errors should name the offending columns so the input can be fixed quickly, especially in ETL/debugging workflows.

## Evidence

- `arnio/convert.py`: `from_dict()` validates the outer object, key types, and nested dictionaries, then calls `pd.DataFrame(data)` directly.
- There is no pre-validation that sequence column values all have the same length.
- Current behavior leaks pandas' generic length error.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import arnio as ar

ar.from_dict({
    "id": [1, 2, 3],
    "name": ["a", "b"],
})
```

## Expected behavior

Arnio should raise a clear error naming the mismatched lengths, for example `from_dict() column lengths differ: id=3, name=2`.

## Actual behavior

The call raises pandas' generic `ValueError: All arrays must be of the same length`.

## Suggested direction

After scalar validation from #1653, validate sequence lengths before constructing the pandas DataFrame. Add tests for two mismatched columns and for a valid equal-length dictionary.

## References

- `arnio/convert.py`

title: Bug: reject unsafe control delimiters in write_csv
body:
## Summary

`write_csv()` allows control-character delimiters such as NUL (`"\0"`) and unit separator (`"\x1f"`). The reader side already treats NUL bytes as binary/corrupted input, so the writer can produce files that Arnio later rejects as invalid CSV.

## Why it matters

CSV writer validation should prevent Arnio from creating output that conflicts with its own reader safety checks. NUL bytes in generated CSV files are especially risky because downstream tools often interpret them as binary/corrupt data.

## Evidence

- `arnio/io.py`: `write_csv()` rejects newline and quote delimiters, but not NUL or other control characters.
- `arnio/io.py`: `_reject_utf8_nul_bytes()` rejects CSV inputs containing NUL bytes.
- Runtime behavior writes NUL-delimited bytes such as `b'a\x00b\n1\x002\n'`.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [2]}))
ar.write_csv(frame, "out.csv", delimiter="\0")
ar.read_csv("out.csv")
```

## Expected behavior

`write_csv()` should reject NUL and other unsafe control-character delimiters with a clear `ValueError` before writing the file.

## Actual behavior

The file is written with NUL bytes, and `read_csv()` later treats the file as binary/corrupted.

## Suggested direction

Reuse or mirror the stricter delimiter validation from CSV reading once #1470 is resolved, and add writer tests for NUL and other control delimiters.

## References

- `arnio/io.py`
- `tests/test_write_csv.py`
- Related reader validation issue: #1470

title: Bug: restrict write_csv line terminators to newline values
body:
## Summary

`write_csv()` accepts arbitrary non-empty `line_terminator` strings such as `"END"` or `"\0"`. This can create files where records are not separated by newline characters, or where NUL bytes are written into the output.

## Why it matters

Line terminators define CSV record boundaries. Allowing arbitrary text makes it easy to generate files that many CSV tools cannot parse, and NUL terminators conflict with Arnio's own binary/corruption checks.

## Evidence

- `arnio/io.py`: `write_csv()` validates `line_terminator` is a non-empty string only.
- Existing validation rejects empty and non-string terminators, but it does not restrict terminators to newline-style values.
- Runtime behavior writes bytes like `b'aEND1END2END'` when `line_terminator="END"`.

## Reproduction or trigger

```python
import pandas as pd
import arnio as ar

frame = ar.from_pandas(pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]}))
ar.write_csv(frame, "out.csv", line_terminator="END")
```

## Expected behavior

`write_csv()` should accept only standard CSV line terminators such as `"\n"`, `"\r\n"`, and possibly `"\r"`, or clearly document broader custom terminators as an advanced escape hatch.

## Actual behavior

Any non-empty string is accepted and written directly between records.

## Suggested direction

Add explicit validation for `line_terminator` values and tests for invalid arbitrary strings and NUL-containing terminators. Keep valid `"\n"` and `"\r\n"` behavior unchanged.

## References

- `arnio/io.py`
- `tests/test_write_csv.py`
- Related closed issues: #576, #577
